opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is where Wittgenstein is so helpful. There's a very natural picture we all fall into, which is that when I understand something, there's the outward stuff, what I say, how I use a word, how I act, and then behind all that there's some inner, private glow of understanding that's the *real* thing. The behaviour is merely evidence for it.

The trouble is that once you've drawn the line that way, you've set yourself up for a kind of permanent scepticism. If the real understanding is hidden in a metaphysically private realm, then nothing anyone does could ever settle whether they understand. Not another person, not an animal, and certainly not a large language model. You've made the question unanswerable in principle, and then you wonder why the debate goes round in circles.

Wittgenstein's point, the way I read him, is not that there's nothing going on inside. Obviously there are mental processes, there are things happening in the brain. The point is that our *concept* of understanding isn't tied to some private inner item. It's woven into a whole public practice: whether you can go on correctly, apply a word in new cases, explain yourself, respond appropriately when challenged. That's what we actually look at when we ask whether someone has understood. Think of the pupil who says "Now I can go on!" The test is whether they can, in fact, go on.

So with AI the useful move is to stop asking, "Is there a little private spark of real understanding in there?" and ask how far the system's behaviour fits the public criteria we normally use, and where it doesn't. Language models are interesting precisely because they meet some of those criteria remarkably well and fail others in quite strange ways. They're exotic, mind-like entities. That's a far more productive conversation than one stuck on an inner essence nobody could ever check. It also keeps us honest in both directions. It stops us dismissing these systems out of hand, and it stops us projecting a rich human inner life onto them just because the words sound fluent.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts public behavior with a supposedly real, metaphysically private inner glow of understanding, expressing the dualistic division.

r002.rationale: It calls this picture natural and says people fall into it, but does not connect that tendency to engaging in philosophy.

r003.rationale: It explains Wittgenstein’s view of understanding, but does not identify overcoming latent dualism as his central challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the trouble starts the moment you picture understanding as having two parts. There's the public part, the stuff we can actually observe: someone uses a word correctly, draws the right inferences, applies a concept in novel situations, corrects themselves when they've made a mistake. And then there's this supposed second component, the private, inner thing, the "real" understanding that's going on behind the scenes, and that in principle nobody else could ever get at.

The Wittgensteinian point, and I'm very much in that tradition, is that once you've set things up that way, the private component does no work at all. If it's genuinely inaccessible, then it can't be what we're tracking when we say of a child, or a colleague, or a chess player, that they understand something. We don't peer into their heads. We look at what they do, over time, in a wide range of circumstances. And in fact, that's all we've ever had to go on, with each other. The grounds for attributing understanding are public through and through.

So the mistake is to think the public criteria are mere evidence for something else, something hidden, rather than being constitutive of what understanding is. The beetle in the box, if you like. It cancels out.

Now, why does this matter for large language models? Because when people say, "Oh, it's just manipulating symbols, there's no real understanding there," they very often have this metaphysically private something in mind. And the irony is that the very same argument would undermine our confidence that other humans understand anything. The sceptic has proven too much.

But I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying the opposite, either, that these systems obviously do understand. What I'm saying is that the question has to be settled by looking at the public criteria, and those criteria are much richer than "it produced a sentence that sounded right." They involve things like robustness, consistency across contexts, the ability to recognise and recover from error, and, crucially, embeddedness in a shared world and a shared form of life, which is where I think current systems are still, let's say, exotic. They're not like us in those respects. So the honest position is that the ordinary concept of understanding was shaped around creatures like us, and when we apply it to something this unfamiliar, we shouldn't be surprised if it starts to fray at the edges. That fraying is interesting. It tells us something about the concept. But it's not a problem that gets fixed by positing a hidden inner light.

r001.rationale: It describes the public/private split as a two-part picture of understanding and calls the supposed inaccessible inner component a mistake, communicating the dualistic framing.

r002.rationale: It does not say that latent dualism is a natural human tendency in philosophical thought.

r003.rationale: It presents a Wittgensteinian objection to the private component, but does not identify overcoming latent dualism as Wittgenstein’s central challenge.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it tempts us into imagining that there are two separate things: the understanding that manifests itself in what somebody says and does, and then some hidden ingredient behind all of that which is the real understanding. And once you’ve set things up that way, you can always ask, ‘But do they really understand?’ regardless of anything they might say or do.

Now, that isn’t to deny that we have an inner life, or that we can understand something without expressing it. The difficulty is with making that inner life metaphysically private—with treating it as something whose connection to our public criteria for understanding is entirely optional.

If you think about how we actually use the word ‘understand’, it has its place in our shared activities. We look at whether someone can explain something, apply it in a new situation, recognise a mistake, and so on. None of those is an infallible test. But they give the concept its substance. If you detach understanding from all of that, it becomes unclear what this additional, hidden property is supposed to amount to.

r001.rationale: It describes the temptation to treat publicly expressed understanding and a hidden, private ingredient as two separate things, conveying the dualistic inclination.

r002.rationale: It says this framing tempts us, but does not claim that latent dualism is a natural human tendency specifically when doing philosophy.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Wittgenstein or identify overcoming latent dualism as his central challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it tempts us into imagining that there are two separate things going on. There’s the public business of using words appropriately, responding to questions, explaining things, and so on. And then there’s this further, hidden ingredient that makes it real understanding, something that could in principle be present or absent without making any difference to any of that.

Now, once you set things up that way, you’ve made that second component inaccessible by definition. And then we start asking whether a machine has it, or even whether another person has it, without having any way of settling the question.

I’d rather look at the role that the concept of understanding plays in our lives. We attribute understanding in a context, on the basis of what someone can do, how they respond, whether they can make connections or recover from a misunderstanding. That doesn’t mean a single convincing utterance establishes understanding. There’s a whole range of circumstances in which the attribution can be tested and revised.

And it doesn’t mean denying that we have an inner life. It means resisting the idea that understanding gets its substance from some metaphysically private thing behind all those capacities. I think that picture creates a mystery rather than helping us understand what understanding is.

r001.rationale: The response describes the distinction as tempting us to imagine two separate things: public capacities and a hidden ingredient that makes understanding real.

r002.rationale: It says the distinction tempts us toward that picture, but does not claim latent dualism is a natural human tendency when engaging in philosophy.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Wittgenstein or identify overcoming latent dualism as his central challenge.
